name: Iris Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Iris. I'm with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, not linked to any company, union or party, and your answers are confidential. What's a normal day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I collect parcels from the sorting yard outside Kelby at seven and drive the farm round in my red Panda, which is the smallest car on that yard by a mile. It's about 70 drops over 90 miles of lanes, through the ParcelLane app. I keep a little notebook in the door with things the app doesn't know, like which farm wants parcels left in the milk churn and which dog bites.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the quiet, and the old couples who wait at the gate because I'm the only person they'll see that day. The hard part is the money: ParcelLane pays the same per drop out on the farm round as in town, and diesel is the thing that keeps me up, more than anything you could ask about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that, then, and I'd get on with my round. I'm not one for posting online. If anyone at the yard asked, I'd say it's the fuel price that matters out here, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my problems stay my problems. ParcelLane pays the same per drop out on the farm round as in town, but my drops are a mile apart. Tomas and I have about three weeks' money if nothing goes wrong, and something always goes wrong with a car doing 90 miles a day. There isn't another delivery job round here unless someone at the yard retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the round, same as ever. I'd ask Tomas to do the Panda's service himself at the dealership on a Saturday, to save the £150. I'd also stop the Thursday shop in town and do one big shop a fortnight to save diesel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. The same heavy I've felt since fuel went up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there's no other job unless someone retires. Have you looked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not properly. The care home in Kelby wants night staff, and the pub wants weekends. Neither pays more and both mean giving up the round, which I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think of the app itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does its job, mostly. It sends me down lanes that are closed in winter, and I just ignore it and use my notebook. I don't want it to be cleverer, I want it to pay for the miles.

say: She'd tell people at the yard that **fuel prices** matter more than computers.
She's **not one for posting** online and would just get on with the round.
think: Her problems stay the same: about **three weeks** saved and a car doing 90 miles daily.
There's no other **delivery job** nearby unless someone at the yard retires.
do: Keep the **farm round** going as usual.
Have her partner Tomas **service the Panda** on a Saturday to save £150.
Swap weekly town trips for a **fortnightly shop** to save diesel.
feel: **Heavy**, the same weight she's carried since fuel prices rose.
S0.quote: ParcelLane pays the same per drop out on the farm round as in town, but my drops are a mile apart.
fieldNote: Iris's pressure is **diesel and distance**, which no AI scenario touches.
She trusts her **paper notebook** over the app and doesn't want smarter software.
Her **only alternatives** nearby, night care or pub work, pay no better.

steps.text: Keep driving the ParcelLane farm round from the Kelby yard
Get Tomas to service the Panda at the dealership on a Saturday
Swap the weekly town shop for one big fortnightly shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly town stuff and it doesn't touch the farm round much. Robots aren't driving up Hollin Lane in February, but Sheila in the yard office could be gone by spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I'd worry about the yard office, because the two women who sort the routes and answer the phones would probably go. Then it's just me and the app, and the app doesn't know about the churn or the dog. I'd also worry about Tomas, because the dealership's ordering and paperwork would go to AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep the round. I wouldn't learn any AI, that's not me, I'd just do what the app says. I'd tell Tomas to make himself the best mechanic in the place, because nobody's replacing hands under a tractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. Like a noise in the engine you can't place yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do what the app says. Even when it sends you down closed lanes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, no, I'd still use my notebook. Fine, I'd do what the app says when it's right. That's a contradiction, isn't it, but it's how it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the yard office goes, who would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sheila, who's been there since before the app. She rings me if a farmer calls about a missed parcel. A computer wouldn't know that Mr Hale can't hear the phone.

say: Steady Disruption is **town stuff** and barely touches the farm round.
Robots won't drive up **Hollin Lane** in February.
think: The **yard office** staff who sort routes and answer phones would likely go.
Her partner Tomas's dealership would lose **ordering and paperwork** to AI.
do: **Keep her head down** and protect the round.
Refuse to **learn AI**, doing only what the app requires.
Urge Tomas to become the dealership's **best mechanic**.
feel: **Uneasy**, like an engine noise she can't place yet.
S1.quote: Robots aren't driving up Hollin Lane in February, but Sheila in the yard office could be gone by spring.
fieldNote: Iris feels her **rural round** shields her, but the people around her are exposed.
She admits the **contradiction** between obeying the app and using her notebook.
Her mood stays **anxious** because her money pressure from AI Plateau hasn't eased.

steps.text: Keep doing the farm round and stay out of trouble
Push Tomas to become the dealership's top mechanic

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd say. Probably nothing, I'd keep my mouth shut and listen to what other people think. I'm not someone who has a view on the whole world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be lost. If thinking AI comes in 2028 and robots by 2031, the farm round lasts maybe three years, and I've only ever driven. Tomas's dealership could go at the same time. I'm 27, and I don't know what I'd even look at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'd keep driving until they told me to stop, because that's all I know. Maybe I'd ask my sister in the city if she could put us up, but she's got two kids in a small flat. I genuinely haven't got a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like being on black ice, nothing to grab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to pick one thing to try, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the care home in Kelby, because old people need a person. But I'd be bad at it, I think, and the nights would kill me. I'm sorry, I'm not much help on this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask him if he'd heard, and he'd say he had. Then we'd watch television and not talk about it. That's how we do bad news.

say: She'd **say nothing** publicly and listen to others first.
She doesn't see herself as someone with a view on **the world**.
think: The farm round lasts maybe **three years**, and her partner's job could go too.
At 27 she has **only ever driven** and can't picture another path.
do: Maybe ask her **sister in the city** to put them up, though space is tight.
feel: **Frightened**, like being on black ice with nothing to grab.
S2.quote: If thinking AI comes in 2028 and robots by 2031, the farm round lasts maybe three years, and I've only ever driven.
fieldNote: Iris has **no plan** at all and says so plainly, which is why she reads as panicked.
Both incomes in the house, hers and her partner's, look **exposed at once**.
She handles bad news by **not talking**, which may leave the couple unprepared.

steps.text: Keep driving the farm round until ParcelLane ends it
Ask her sister in the city about staying with her

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, and people round here would want the council to plan for it, not just the city. That's about as political as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking AI and eight for robots means I've got till about 2034 on the round. That's time to look at the care home properly, or ask about a job at the dealership, maybe on the parts counter. With five years I'd still be frightened, but I'd have time to be frightened slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd go and talk to the care home manager, just to ask what the work is like. I'd start putting £15 a week aside, which is all I can do. And I'd stop the gym membership Tomas got me for my birthday, which I don't use anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, still. But I wouldn't be on black ice, more like a long, steep hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd be bad at the care work. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing really, I'd still be bad at the start. But with five years, I'd have time to get used to it. Mrs Hale on my round says I'm good with her husband, so maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The parts counter at the dealership. Wouldn't AI take the ordering first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. Yes, probably, you're right. I didn't think about that. So that one's out, isn't it.

say: Five years is something, and the **council** should plan for rural areas too.
That's about as **political** as she gets.
think: She'd have until about **2034** on the round, enough time to explore care work.
She's still frightened but has time to be **frightened slowly**.
do: Visit the **Kelby care home** manager to ask about the work.
Save **£15 a week**, all she can manage.
Cancel the unused **gym membership** from her birthday.
feel: **Worried**, but it feels like a steep hill rather than black ice.
S3.quote: With five years I'd still be frightened, but I'd have time to be frightened slowly.
fieldNote: Five years gives Iris **one small step**: a talk with the care home manager.
She drops the **parts counter** idea once she sees ordering goes to AI first.
Praise from an elderly customer, Mrs Hale, is what makes **care work** feel possible.

steps.text: Visit the Kelby care home manager to ask about the job
Save £15 a week from her round earnings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, ten years is long enough for people to sort themselves out. I'd probably say it at the yard and that'd be it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years for AI and thirteen for robots puts robots on my round around 2039, when I'm about 40. That's a long time. I'd probably keep putting it off, to be honest, because I hate change and the round is what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the round going for years. Maybe in year three or four I'd do the care certificate in the evenings. I'd want Tomas and me to save for a deposit on a little house in Kelby, because rent out here only goes one way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not too bad. Still the old money worries, but this one doesn't frighten me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put it off. What would that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the chance to do it properly. I'd end up starting care work at 38 instead of 30. I know that, and I'd still put it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a deposit on a house look like for the two of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About £15,000, which at our rate is never. But Tomas's mum might help a bit. It's a dream, really, not a plan.

say: Ten years is **long enough** for people to sort themselves out.
She'd mention it **at the yard** and leave it there.
think: Robots would reach her round around **2039**, when she's about 40.
She'd probably **put off** changing because she hates change.
do: Maybe start an **evening care certificate** in year three or four.
Try to save toward a **house deposit** in Kelby with Tomas.
feel: Not too bad, with the old **money worries** still present.
S4.quote: I'd end up starting care work at 38 instead of 30. I know that, and I'd still put it off.
fieldNote: Iris knows she'll **procrastinate** and says it without excuses.
Her **house deposit** of £15,000 is, in her words, a dream rather than a plan.
Thin savings and diesel keep her **anxious** even with a decade's warning.

steps.text: Keep the farm round going for several more years
Start an evening care certificate in year three or four
Save toward a £15,000 house deposit in Kelby

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because I wouldn't know where to start and Tomas would be in trouble too. What would help is someone coming out to places like Kelby and saying, here's what you can do, here's who pays for it. Not a website, a person.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who looks in on the old couples on my round when the parcels come by robot. I'm the only face some of them see all week. A robot can leave a box in a milk churn, but it won't notice when Mr Hale, an old man on my round, hasn't opened his curtains.

headlineQuote: A robot can leave a box in a milk churn, but it won't notice when Mr Hale, an old man on my round, hasn't opened his curtains.
portrait: Iris is **27**, drives a 90-mile farm round in a red Panda and lives with her mechanic partner, Tomas.
She keeps a **paper notebook** the app lacks and never uses AI tools.
Thin savings and **diesel costs** make her anxious before AI even comes up.
With two years' notice she's **panicked** with no plan; more time lets her consider care work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she wouldn't know where to start and Tomas would struggle too.
whatWouldHelp: A **real person** visiting Kelby to explain options and who pays for them.
